Text.Text: Nothing left to teach. The range is honest again and the name's yours now. Wear it quiet.
Holster's worn wrong. You lean on that pistol; you don't live in it yet. Come back when it answers before you've finished asking.

Holster's worn right. That buys you one conversation. Out the west trail there's a canyon range I marshaled for twenty years, and a crew is running a school on my name there. Last Word, taught by men who never heard one. Six of their adepts hold the near stretch. Put them down and bring me the Last Word Canyon Range Tally they keep score on.
Key's yours. Cliff door in the Rocky Pass, near stretch, six adepts. Don't come back with almost.
A duel is an argument. Most men make their point loud and long. The last word is one shot, and it ends the argument. It isn't the fastest shot. It's the one that doesn't miss.

Take the west trail out of here into the Rocky Pass. The door is a short walk south of where the trail comes in, against the pass's east bank. My key fits it. Watch the high walls in there. Sound lies in that canyon.
Adepts. Young, fast, sloppy. They'll fan wide and talk to make you draw first. Don't. Six funerals, one conversation.
Six adepts still breathing and my tally still in their hands. The argument isn't over till it's over.
You walk quieter than you did. That's the range teaching. Let's see the tally.
Six lines, all closed. Pay buys ammunition. The lesson is the part you keep.

You came back. The adepts didn't. Next problem: five specialists working the long lanes deeper in. They've dialed my old sightlines into ambush work. Put all five down and bring back the Last Word Sightline Calibrator before they teach the rock itself to cheat.
Long lanes, five shooters. Walk soft, shoot once.
I marshaled duels on that range for twenty years. When I hung it up, my best students didn't. They sell Last Word to anyone with coin and a grudge. Every graduate is a murder with my signature on it.
That calibrator zeroed the lanes for honest duels. In their hands it zeroes bushwhack angles. Bring it back and the canyon goes back to lying equally to everyone.
Specialists don't miss twice. They'll hold the long lanes and let the suns do half the work. Keep rock at your back and make your first shot the whole conversation.
Five specialists, still shooting. My calibrator, still theirs. The long lanes are waiting on your answer.
Heard the long lanes go quiet. Five funerals' worth of quiet. Show me the calibrator.
Zeroed and honest again. You shoot like the argument's already over. They've noticed. Good.

Now the warden. He keeps the trial altar in the middle of the range, and he was the best I ever passed. Wears my crest like he earned all of it. Break him and bring me what's left of it, the Last Word Shattered Range Crest. And hear this plain: I'd take two guns I trust through that door. So will you.
One more thing. Pride is a caliber that never stopped anybody. Bring the friends.

Trained him. Vouched for him. He was patient when the rest were fast, and patience is the whole discipline. Then he learned patience collects better as a toll than a duty. He's still patient. That's the problem.
The trial altar, middle of the range. He's scratched a firing line into the floor there and takes every challenge from it. He'll know you're coming. He always knows.

Help. Yes. The warden's put faster hands than yours in the ground, one at a time, because they came one at a time. Bring two guns you trust and hand him three arguments at once. Even his patience can't answer all of them.
Warden's still standing and my crest is still on his chest. Middle of the range, at the altar. Three of you. I meant that.
You're standing here. Means he isn't standing anywhere. The crest.
Shattered. Fitting. He carried it wrong and it carried him nowhere. His toll road is closed, and that canyon gets its first honest night in years.

Four left that matter. The inner circle, the ones who ran the school after they buried my name in it. They bank a challenge chit that used to mean something: lay it on the marshal's table and the marshal must answer. Kill the four and bring me the Last Word Marshal's Challenge Chit. We're going to use it properly.
Four of them, spread across the range. Shoot the polite one first. He's the signal.

Two washed out of my classes, two never sat them. Between them they've graduated ten years of duelists who think a fast draw is a verdict. Killing the four won't undo that. It stops the printing press.

Old range law. Any shooter lays that chit on the marshal's table, the marshal answers. No seconds, no tolls, no terms. They keep it locked up because the man at the top doesn't take challenges anymore. We're going to renew the tradition.
Together, and from four directions. They fought as a circle long before they ran one. Whoever stood with you against the warden, bring them again. And watch the corners.
Four of the circle still walk the range, and the chit's still in their strongbox. Arguments don't settle themselves.
Four chairs empty at their table. Arithmetic I like. The chit.
You know what this buys. I'll post it on the marshal's board myself; some rights I kept. He'll answer. Rest first. You'll want steady hands for the introduction.

Chit's posted. He answered. Understand what's waiting: the master has the real Last Word, the shot that ends arguments, the thing you've been circling this whole climb. He has never lost one. He'll meet you in the Canyon Dueling Pit, through the door at the north end of the range. Take your two friends; nobody walks out of that pit alone. Nobody ever has.
No advice left worth giving. Except this. He'll offer you the first word. Don't take it. Take the last.

My last student. I gave him the discipline whole because he was the only one who could hold it. He held it, then he sold it. Every grave that school dug traces back to a lesson I taught. This argument was always half mine.
The Canyon Dueling Pit, through the door at the north end of the range. He'll meet you in the open. He's not a coward. That would be easier.

Like the argument ended before you drew, and everything after is paperwork. He'll spend the first exchange reading you, and most don't survive the reading. Three of you is three stories at once. That's your opening. It's the only one.
Master's still in the Dueling Pit and the challenge is still open. Arguments age badly. So does he. Finish it.
Word came in on the west trail ahead of you. The canyon's gone quiet. Say the words.
Then the name is yours. Last Word, worn by somebody who earned it, and I'm done being the last who did. Take the pay, buy your two friends whatever they drink, and keep that holster worn right.

Two pistols? Most people just make twice the noise. Show me that each hand can hold its own rhythm, and we'll talk about Twin Suns. Take this canyon range key. At the Anchorhead Canyon Range, keep both guns on one hostile range enemy: twelve ordinary hits within thirty seconds, at least six from each gun. Abilities don't count. Change enemies or swap a gun and you start again.
One steady horizon. That's the trick. Your strong hand can't drag the other along, and a fancy burst won't hide a weak rhythm. Keep both working when the target shoots back.
Choose a range enemy that can survive the exercise. Ordinary shots from both guns must land; misses use time but don't erase your hits. Stay on that enemy, and keep the pair equipped.
From Anchorhead's Southern Entrance, take the west trail into the Rocky Pass. The sealed cliff door just south of the trail leads into the Canyon Range. The key opens it.
Key's yours. Two hands, one enemy. Bring me a clean firing trace.
The range recorder hasn't caught a clean sequence yet. Twelve ordinary hits, six from each gun, on one range enemy within thirty seconds.
That's a clean trace. Neither hand hid behind the other. Ready to put your name to it?
Twin Suns is yours to learn. Spend the training points when you're ready; approval alone won't pull the triggers for you.
Learn the pair first. Reach rank fifty in Twin Pistol, then I'll test whether both hands answer.
Back to the adepts.
Six adepts. I'll bring your tally.
What is the Last Word?
How do I get in?
What am I walking into?
Not today.
Their tally. Six lines closed.
Back to the specialists.
Five specialists. Consider it argued.
Who are these people?
Why does the calibrator matter?
How do specialists fight?
Give me a day.
Your calibrator. The lanes are quiet.
Back to the warden.
Then the warden falls. I won't go alone.
You trained him?
Where does he hold?
You think I need help?
Not until I'm ready.
His crest. It broke when he did.
Back to the circle.
Four names. I'll bring the chit.
Who are the four?
What does the chit actually do?
How will they come at me?
Not yet.
The chit. Their table's cleared.
Back to the master.
Then it's the last argument. We'll settle it.
Who is he to you?
Where does he wait?
How does a man who never lost fight?
Not yet. Not for this.
The argument's over. For good.
What can you teach me about Twin Pistol?
I'll hold the rhythm.
Why ordinary shots?
What makes a clean attempt?
Where is the range?
Both guns held the same horizon.
I'll keep practicing.
